# The Juiciest Corporate Scandals with Becca Platsky

First listed: 2026-08-26 | Evaluation cutoff: 2026-11-10

[Back to library](../README.md)

## Source versions

- [Substack: The Juiciest Corporate Scandals with Becca Platsky](https://realeismanplaybook.substack.com/p/the-juiciest-corporate-scandals-with) - 2026-08-26

Earliest listed publication among matched versions, not proof of an unedited contemporaneous archive. Claim timestamps refer to the reviewed version.

## Summary

Eisman and Platsky use fraud cases, media mergers, prediction markets and FIFA to discuss oversight and executive accountability. Platsky corrects her Frank customer counts during the interview. Eisman favors the Paramount combination and challenges weak corporate governance, but makes overbroad claims about the absence of financial-crisis prosecutions. Official records verify the Javice case and contemporaneous merger delay, correct Immelt tenure, and contradict claims of universal executive impunity. Many psychological explanations, private anecdotes and current corruption allegations remain unverified.

Valuable governance questions with uneven factual precision. Preserve explicit corrections and distinguish subjective criticism from legal findings. Guest allegations are not Eisman views by silence. His broad enforcement language conflicts with documented prosecutions, while the narrower accountability of leading Wall Street executives remains unresolved.

## Framework and tools

- Compare public executive statements with filings and actual conduct.
- Separate fraud identification from short-sale timing.
- Distinguish buyer due diligence failures from perpetrator culpability.
- Test board independence and relevant expertise.
- Use pressure, opportunity and rationalization as risk questions, not proof of guilt.
- Distinguish allegations, charges, convictions and policy preferences.

Tools and charts discussed, not a complete visual inspection:

- Trial and sentencing records
- Acquisition customer data and due-diligence verification
- Merger market capitalization comparisons
- Ticking-fee provisions and litigation calendar
- Executive compensation and tenure
- Board biographies and family relationships
- Fraud triangle
- White-collar prosecution counts
